title: Gandhari's blindfold
hookLine: the pale one is crowned, and a princess learns her groom is blind and takes a vow with a strip of cloth
carry: a vrata: a hardship chosen for love
tomorrow: a king out hunting shoots a deer, and the deer speaks.

cards: A strip of cloth, folded over and over, tied behind the head. A young princess named Gandhari, from the land of Gandhara, has been promised to a prince of the Kurus. Then she learns that he is blind.
She takes a cloth, folds it, and binds her own eyes. Before we get to why, see the boys grow up.

teach.b: First, the boys grow up. Bhishma raises them as his own. Dhritarashtra becomes the strongest, Pandu the finest archer, and Vidura knows dharma best.
The eldest is blind, so the text says the crown passes to Pandu. Then Bhishma asks for Gandhari, princess of Gandhara, as Dhritarashtra's bride. Her family hesitates over a blind groom, then agrees.
When Gandhari hears, she folds a cloth and binds her eyes, resolving, the text says, never to have more than her husband has. Her brother, Shakuni, brings her to Hastinapura. Remember his name.
Retellings call the blindfold her vow, and Hindus have a word for a vow like that: vrata.

A vrata is a hardship you choose to take on, usually for God or for someone you love: a fast, a silence, giving something up. It's one of the most common practices in Hindu homes today. Some fast on Mondays for Shiva.
Many married women keep Karva Chauth, fasting from sunrise until the moon rises, praying for their husband's long life. Readers still argue about Gandhari's vow. Some see complete devotion.

Some see a quiet protest at a marriage she didn't choose. Some see grief. All of them treat it as her choice, and that's the heart of a vrata: nobody can take it for you, and nobody should force it on you.
Today a vrata can be small: going without something you love, on a day you pray for someone, and meaning it.

how: Vratas, chosen vows like a weekly fast or Karva Chauth, are kept in many Hindu homes. Gandhari is remembered in retellings as a figure of pativrata, devotion to a husband, and her blindfold is the image tellers and painters use for a vow kept for life.

games.q: your aunt is keeping Karva Chauth and a cousin says 'that's just suffering for nothing.' by Gandhari's story, what's closest?
o: it's a vrata: a hardship she chose, offered for someone she loves.
it's a rule wives must follow, whether they want to or not.
it's a diet thing with a religious name.
games.why: a vrata is chosen. readers still argue about Gandhari's vow, but it was hers. that's what gives a vrata its meaning.

practice: Pick one small thing you could go without today, a snack, your phone at dinner, one show, and one person you'll hold in mind while you do. If you pray, offer it to God for them. If you don't, let it be a quiet gift.
Keep it small and kind; a vrata isn't a punishment.
